topic.name: The Gradient as a Normal Vector

question.text: Consider the plane curve $2xy + 6y^2 = x -2.$ Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(8, -3).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side: \begin{align} 2xy + 6y^2 &= x -2 \\[3pt] 2xy + 6y^2 -x&= -2 \end{align}

If we set $f(x,y) = 2xy + 6y^2 -x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(8,-3)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(8,-3).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(8,-3)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x(x,y) \, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} ( 2xy + 6y^2 -x) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} ( 2xy + 6y^2 -x) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= (2y-1) \, \mathbf i + (2 x + 12 y) \, \mathbf j \\[7pt] \nabla f(8,-3) &= (2(-3)-1) \, \mathbf i + (2(8)+12(-3)) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= -7 \, \mathbf i -20 \, \mathbf j \\[3pt] &= \langle -7, -20 \rangle \end{align*}

Hence, $\nabla f(8,-3)= \langle -7, -20 \rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(8,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x-x_0}{v_x} &= \dfrac{y-y_0}{v_y} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x-8}{-7} &= \dfrac{y-(-3)}{-20} \\[5pt] -20(x-8) &=-7( y+3) \\[5pt] -20x+7y+160+21 &= 0 \\[5pt] -20x+7y+181 &= 0 \end{align*}

question.text: Consider the plane curve $2x+y-1 = \sqrt{x^2-y^2}.$ Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,0).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side: \begin{align} 2x+y-1 &= \sqrt{x^2-y^2} \\[3pt] -1 &= \sqrt{x^2-y^2} - 2x - y \end{align}

If we set $f(x,y) = \sqrt{x^2-y^2} - 2x - y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x(x,y) \, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left(\sqrt{x^2-y^2} - 2x - y\right) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\sqrt{x^2-y^2} - 2x - y\right) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2-y^2}}-2\right) \, \mathbf i + \left(-\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2-y^2}}-1\right) \, \mathbf j \\[7pt] \nabla f(1,0) &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1^2-0^2}}-2\right) \, \mathbf i + \left(-\dfrac{0}{\sqrt{1^2-0^2}}-1\right) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= - \mathbf i - \mathbf j \\[3pt] &= \langle -1, -1 \rangle \end{align*}

Hence, $\nabla f(1,0)= \langle -1, -1 \rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x-x_0}{v_x} &= \dfrac{y-y_0}{v_y} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x-1}{-1} &= \dfrac{y-0}{-1} \\[5pt] 1-x &= -y \\[5pt] x-y &= 1 \end{align*}

question.text: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $3x^2-xz = 6 - 3xyz$ at the point $(1,0,-3).$
question.explanation:
First, we bring all variables to one side: \begin{align*} 3x^2-xz &= 6-3xyz \\[3pt] 3x^2-xz+3xyz &= 6 \end{align*}

If we set $f(x,y,z) = 3x^2-xz+3xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,-3)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,0,-3).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,-3)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) & = f_x(x,y,z)\, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} \left( 3x^2-xz+3xyz \right) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left( 3x^2-xz+3xyz \right) \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} \left( 3x^2-xz+3xyz \right) \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= (6x-z+3yz) \ \mathbf i + 3xz \ \mathbf j +(-x+3xy) \ \mathbf k \\[7pt] \nabla f(1, 0, -3) &= (6(1)-(-3)+3(0)(-3)) \ \mathbf i + 3(1)(-3) \ \mathbf j + (-1+3(1)(0)) \ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= 9\, \mathbf i - 9 \, \mathbf j - \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \langle 9, -9, -1 \rangle \end{align*}

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf v = \langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be written as:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{x - x_0}{v_x} = \dfrac{y - y_0}{v_y} = \dfrac{z - z_0}{v_z} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x - 1}{9} = \dfrac{y - 0}{-9} = \dfrac{z - (-3)}{-1} \\[5pt] \dfrac{x-1}{9} = \dfrac{y}{-9} = \dfrac{z + 3}{-1} \end{align*}

question.text: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = \arctan{\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (2, -2).$
question.explanation:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y) = (2,-2)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,-2).$

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (2,-2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y) &= f_x(x,y) \, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y) \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left(\arctan{\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)}\right) \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} \left(\arctan{\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)}\right) \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{y}{x^2}\right)}{1+\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)^2} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)}{1+\left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)^2} \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{y}{x^2+y^2} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2} \, \mathbf j\\[7pt] \nabla f(2,-2) &=-\dfrac{(-2)}{2^2+(-2)^2} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{2}{2^2+(-2)^2} \, \mathbf j \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{8} \, \mathbf i + \dfrac{2}{8} \, \mathbf j\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \left( \mathbf i + \mathbf j\right) \end{align*}

Finally, we normalize $\nabla f(2,-2)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} \dfrac{\nabla f(2,-2)}{\| \nabla f(2,-2) \|} & = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{4}(\mathbf i + \mathbf j)}{\left\| \dfrac{1}{4}(\mathbf i + \mathbf j)\right\|}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2}\right)} \cdot \dfrac{1}{4}(\mathbf i + \mathbf j)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\mathbf i + \mathbf j)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} (\mathbf i + \mathbf j). \end{align}

question.text: For the function $f(x,y,z) = x^2 - 2yz +xyz$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (1,2,-1).$
question.explanation:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (1,2,-1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,2,-1).$

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (1,2,-1)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x,y,z) & = f_x(x,y,z)\, \mathbf i + f_y(x,y,z)\ \mathbf j + f_z(x,y,z)\ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (x^2 - 2yz +xyz) \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (x^2 - 2yz +xyz) \, \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} (x^2 - 2yz +xyz) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = (2x + yz)\, \mathbf i + (-2z+xz) \, \mathbf j + (-2y+xy) \, \mathbf k\\[7pt] \nabla f(1,2,-1) & = (2(1) + (2)(-1))\, \mathbf i + (-2(-1)+(1)(-1)) \, \mathbf j + (-2(2)+(1)(2)) \, \mathbf k \\[5pt] & = \mathbf j - 2 \, \mathbf k \end{align*}

Therefore, $\, \mathbf j - 2 \, \mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (1,2,-1).$
